subject: ent
title: Dysphagia and the Oesophagus

steps.tx: **Zenker diverticulum** is a pharyngeal pouch that herniates posteriorly through Killian dehiscence between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus in elderly patients, as incoordination raises hypopharyngeal pressure. Undigested food regurgitation hours after meals, gurgling in the neck, halitosis, recurrent chest infection and weight loss form the presentation. A neck swelling that gurgles on palpation, Boyce sign, supports the diagnosis at the bedside.
steps.say: Posterior herniation through the weak constrictor gap gives a pouch in elderly patients. Regurgitation of undigested food hours later with neck gurgling indicates pouch disease. Chest infection from spillover is part of the classic presentation pattern.

vis.alt: Pharyngeal pouch diagram with outpouching through the Killian gap and a barium swallow image.
vis.caption: Zenker pouch through the Killian gap. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Killian dehiscence** anatomy decides both pouch formation and surgical danger, because the pouch neck sits above the cricopharyngeal bar that fails to relax in coordination with pharyngeal contraction. Barium swallow shows the posterior sac filling beside the cervical oesophagus, often with overflow aspiration. Endoscopy must be cautious because the instrument preferentially enters the pouch and perforation follows blind advancement against its wall.
steps.say: Failed sphincter relaxation against pharyngeal contraction produces the pouch above the bar. Barium studies give the posterior sac image with overflow aspiration risk. Blind advancement is dangerous because the instrument passes into the pouch and perforation follows.

steps.tx: **Cricopharyngeal achalasia** is failure of the upper sphincter to relax adequately, producing cervical dysphagia, nasal regurgitation incoordination symptoms and pouch formation when chronic. Manometry and swallow studies separate primary sphincter failure from neurological causes such as stroke or motor neurone disease. Treatment divides the cricopharyngeus by endoscopic stapling or laser myotomy, sharing the operation that also treats established Zenker pouches.
steps.say: Sphincter relaxation failure produces cervical dysphagia and pouch formation when chronic. Swallow studies separate primary failure from neurological causes such as stroke. Division of the muscle provides treatment for both sphincter failure and pouch.

steps.tx: **Achalasia cardia** is the lower sphincter counterpart, where oesophageal aperistalsis and failed lower sphincter relaxation give progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids together, regurgitation and weight loss. Barium shows a smooth tapered bird beak narrowing with dilated oesophagus above, contrasting malignant irregular shouldering. The comparison teaches a general rule: benign strictures taper smoothly, malignant strictures shoulder irregularly and progress over weeks in older patients.
steps.say: Lower sphincter failure gives dysphagia to solids and liquids together from onset. Smooth tapered narrowing indicates benign achalasia on barium studies. Irregular shouldering with rapid progression indicates malignancy instead.

steps.tx: **Foreign body oesophagus** lodges classically at the cricopharynx, the narrowest point, where a swallowed coin in a child or fish bone in an adult produces drooling, dysphagia and neck tenderness. Button batteries are the emergency exception, causing liquefactive necrosis within hours and needing immediate removal regardless of symptoms. Sharp objects and complete obstruction with drooling also bypass observation queues and go directly to rigid endoscopy.
steps.say: Swallowed objects lodge at the cricopharynx and produce drooling with dysphagia. Button batteries cause rapid tissue necrosis and require immediate removal always. Sharp objects with complete obstruction need direct rigid endoscopy.

steps.tx: A **coin at cricopharynx** shows on frontal radiograph as a round opacity face on, while its sagittal orientation separates oesophageal coins from tracheal coins that align differently and threaten airway. Lateral imaging confirms level and excludes multiple objects. Removal uses rigid oesophagoscopy under general anaesthesia with airway control, after which the mucosa is inspected for battery injury, sharp trauma or underlying stricture that invited impaction.
steps.say: Frontal films give oesophageal coins a face on appearance at the cricopharyngeal level. Orientation separates airway coins that threaten breathing immediately. Mucosal inspection after removal excludes injury and underlying stricture.

steps.tx: **Corrosive stricture** follows alkali or acid ingestion after the acute burn heals into fibrotic narrowing over weeks, producing progressive solid dysphagia months later in many survivors. Long or multiple strictures resist dilatation and may need oesophageal replacement by gastric or colonic conduit in severe cases. Early endoscopy grading after ingestion predicts stricture risk and forbids blind tube passage through necrotic wall in the acute phase.
steps.say: Healed corrosive burns produce fibrotic narrowing with progressive solid dysphagia months later. Long strictures resist dilatation and sometimes require conduit replacement surgery. Early burn grading predicts stricture risk after ingestion.

steps.tx: A rigid metal tube advanced under direct vision is **rigid oesophagoscopy**. The surgeon sees the wall as the scope passes, so a pouch, a sharp foreign body, or a hypopharyngeal lesion can be inspected and biopsied. The instrument moves only while the lumen is in view, because a blind push can perforate the piriform fossa or the cervical oesophagus. Neck crepitus, chest pain, or fever afterwards means perforation until a contrast study excludes it. Flexible endoscopy is gentler for diagnosis, but the rigid scope still removes many sharp foreign bodies.
steps.say: Rigid oesophagoscopy passes a metal tube under direct vision so a pouch, a foreign body, or a hypopharyngeal lesion can be seen and biopsied. The lumen must stay in view, or the piriform fossa and cervical oesophagus can be perforated. Crepitus, chest pain, or fever after the examination is treated as a perforation until contrast imaging excludes it.

vis.alt: A rigid oesophagoscope is shown passing under direct vision to inspect the esophageal wall.
vis.caption: The rigid metal tube advances only while the oesophageal lumen is in view. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Rigid oesophagoscopy** remains the therapeutic instrument for sharp foreign bodies, proximal impactions and biopsy of upper lesions, demanding neck extension positioning and respect for pyriform and cricopharyngeal injury points. Flexible endoscopy suits most diagnostic work and distal therapy with less perforation risk. Perforation signs after either instrument, surgical emphysema, chest pain and fever, trigger water soluble contrast study and broad cover without oral intake.
steps.say: Rigid instruments provide treatment for sharp proximal impactions under general anaesthesia with airway control. Flexible instruments are suitable for most diagnostic work with lower perforation risk. Chest pain with emphysema after instrumentation requires perforation workup urgently.

vis.alt: Pharyngeal pouch anatomy diagram showing the pouch neck above the cricopharyngeal bar.
vis.caption: Pouch neck anatomy guiding endoscopy. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Sideropenic dysphagia** is the dysphagia of iron deficiency with oesophageal webs in Plummer Vinson syndrome, relieved partly by iron correction and web dilatation when needed. Its postcricoid cancer association, covered in the cancer lesson, makes webs a surveillance finding rather than a curiosity. Any web in an older patient with anaemia therefore earns upper endoscopy with careful postcricoid inspection at the same sitting.
steps.say: Iron deficiency webs produce dysphagia that iron correction and dilatation relieve partly. Cancer association makes webs a surveillance finding in older patients. Endoscopy includes careful postcricoid inspection at the same sitting.

steps.tx: **Globus pharyngeus** is the lump in throat sensation without true dysphagia, typically between meals, eased by swallowing food and worsened by dry swallows, stress and throat clearing. Normal examination and absence of red flags allow reflux and anxiety based management without exhaustive imaging. True dysphagia, weight loss, anaemia or referred ear pain removes globus from consideration and restarts the structural workup immediately.
steps.say: Lump sensation without true dysphagia that eases with food indicates globus typically. Normal examination without red flags allows reflux based management safely. True dysphagia or weight loss needs structural workup immediately.

steps.tx: **Barium swallow** remains the first structural test for dysphagia localisation, pouch, achalasia pattern and stricture shape, while endoscopy provides biopsy and therapy and manometry resolves motility questions. Choosing the sequence by suspected level saves time: cervical symptoms image the pharynx, retrosternal sticking scopes the oesophagus, and liquid plus solid failure studies motility. Red flag dysphagia in older patients goes to endoscopy first regardless of barium elegance.
steps.say: Barium studies localise pouches and stricture shapes while endoscopy provides biopsy capability. Motility studies are used after structure is cleared for liquid and solid failure patterns. Red flag dysphagia in older patients requires endoscopy first.

cards.b: Elderly regurgitation hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling neck swelling (Boyce sign); pouch through Killian dehiscence on barium.
Oesophageal button battery needs immediate removal; liquefactive necrosis begins within hours.
Benign tapers smoothly (bird beak in achalasia); malignant shoulders irregularly with rapid progression.

keys: Coin orientation separates oesophagus from trachea
Globus has no true dysphagia and no red flags
